His father died when he was three. At 23 he left home to become a monk of the Lebanese Maronite Order and took the name Charbel. He was ordained a priest on July 23, 1859. For many years he lived in the community at the Monastery of Saint Maron at Annaya. From 1875 he lived as a hermit nearby, in prayer, fasting and manual work. He died on December 24, 1898, eight days after he was taken ill while celebrating Mass. Crowds came to his tomb afterward, Christians and Muslims alike. He studied Arabic, French and Syriac at the College de la Sagesse in Beirut, then went to Alexandria in 1892 to teach Arabic - and there, far from home, heard the call to the priesthood. The next year he entered the Capuchin convent of Khashbau, back in his own hills, and on November 1, 1901, he was ordained a priest in Beirut. Lebanon knew him simply as Abouna Yaacoub - Father Jacob. From 1903 to 1914 he walked Lebanon on foot with a knapsack on his shoulder, preaching in village after village - and became known as the Apostle of Lebanon . Bekaa Kafra sits at about 1,800 meters above sea level in the Bsharri district of North Lebanon - widely known as the highest village in the country. Its name is Syriac: bekaa , ground, and kafra , rich - "rich soil." It overlooks the holy valley of Qannoubine, which sheltered twenty-four Maronite patriarchs between 1440 and 1823 along with generations of hermits and monks, and it neighbors the Cedars of God. The village's own history reaches back at least to the tenth century by the historian Fouad Boustany Ephram's account, and its houses still keep their modest old architecture. Youssef Antoun Makhlouf was born here, traditionally on May 8, 1828, the youngest of five children of Antoun Zaarour Makhlouf and Brigitta Chidiac. Maronite History Charbel's Life St Nimatullah Our principal source for Maroun's life is Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus (393-466), who wrote about him within a generation of his death in the Religious History of Syriac Asceticism . Maroun had been a disciple of the hermit Zebinas, a man known for praying day and night. Seeking solitude, Maroun chose the top of a mountain - probably south of Cyrrhus and northwest of Aleppo, in what is now Syria - a place that had been sacred to pagans. There he found a pagan temple, and converted it into a church dedicated to the true God. His austerity was striking even by the standards of Syrian monasticism. He pitched a small tent for shelter but rarely used it, choosing to live in the open air as a form of mortification. He would often spend the whole night standing in prayer, fasted for weeks on end, and - Theodoret tells us - was not satisfied with the ordinary exercises of piety but added to them. Arabic-speaking Christians call them Mar Sarkis and Bakhos. They were not Lebanese, but the Maronite Church honors them, and one of the oldest monasteries above the Qadisha Valley carries their name. Children's storybook St Maroun All saints Sarkis and Bakhos are the Arabic names of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, two Roman army officers martyred in Syria about 303. Their feast is 7 October. The Church counts them as martyrs of the early centuries, honored in the East and the West. They are not Lebanese saints: the Maronite Church venerates them, and the Maronite monastery of Mar Sarkis and Bakhos at Ehden is dedicated to them. The faith is worth more than the favor of the powerful, and it is easier to keep with a friend beside you. The old account has the two officers answer that nothing is gained by winning the world and losing one's soul, echoing Matthew 16:26. Where it comes from: the Passion of Sergius and Bacchus, probably written in the 5th century. The Catholic Encyclopedia treats the martyrdom as well authenticated and the details of the Passion as legend, so we tell the teaching as the tradition's, not as a record.
